PMGT1711 Week 03

PMGT1711 Week 03 - Complex Adaptive Systems and Causal Loop Diagrams

Overview

This week introduces the core vocabulary of complexity and the basic tool for mapping feedback structure:

• Complex adaptive systems (CAS) and their defining properties: emergence, self-organisation and the edge of chaos.

• Structural complexity and the three factors that make a situation complex: quantity, interconnectedness and ambiguity.

• An introduction to system dynamics, the modelling of how quantities in a system change and feed back over time.

• Causal loop diagrams (CLDs): how to draw causal links with polarity marks, how to recognise a reinforcing loop (R) and a balancing loop (B), and how to classify a loop by counting its negative links.

Key Concepts

Complex adaptive systems

A complex adaptive system (CAS) is a system whose parts are agents that learn and adapt their behaviour as they interact, so the system's behaviour is produced by the interactions rather than designed in advance. Three properties are central:

• Emergence: large-scale patterns or behaviours appear from the local interactions of the parts, without anyone designing or controlling them.

• Self-organisation: the system develops structure and order on its own, without an external controller arranging it.

• Edge of chaos: the regime between rigid order (which freezes the system) and pure chaos (which destroys structure), where the system is flexible enough to adapt and produce novelty.

A system that merely shows emergence is not automatically a complete CAS: the presence of learning, adapting agents is essential.

Complexity and its three factors

Complexity is the property of a situation that makes its behaviour hard to predict or control. It has three contributing factors:

• Quantity (number of elements): how many parts, variables or stakeholders the situation contains.

• Interconnectedness: how strongly and how densely the elements affect one another.

• Ambiguity: how unclear or open to multiple interpretations the elements and their relationships are.

Complexity is often expressed as a combination of these three: number of elements multiplied by interconnectedness and ambiguity. A situation with many elements, dense connections and high ambiguity is the hardest to manage.

Reinforcing and balancing loops

Feedback loops are the engines of system behaviour:

• A reinforcing loop (R) amplifies whatever change is happening. It can amplify growth, and it can equally amplify decline - amplification is not the same as improvement.

• A balancing loop (B) counteracts change and pushes the system back towards a target or equilibrium.

Frameworks and Formulas

Causal loop diagram conventions

A causal loop diagram (CLD) shows variables as nodes and causal influences as arrows. Each arrow is labelled with its polarity - whether the cause and the effect move in the same or opposite directions - and each loop is labelled R or B. Polarity describes the direction of causation, not whether the effect is good or bad.

Symbol

Meaning

S or +

Same-direction causation: when the cause increases, the effect increases; when the cause decreases, the effect decreases

O or -

Opposite-direction causation: when the cause increases, the effect decreases, and vice versa

Double slash (//) drawn across an arrow

A delay: the effect of the cause is felt only after a time lag

Classifying a loop: the negative-link rule

To decide whether a closed loop is reinforcing or balancing, count the negative (O / -) links in the loop:

• An even number of negative links (including zero) means the loop is reinforcing (R).

• An odd number of negative links means the loop is balancing (B).

The logic: each negative link reverses the direction of change once. A loop that reverses the direction an even number of times (or not at all) returns to the original direction, so a change reinforces itself; an odd number of reversals makes the loop push back against the change, so it balances.

Drawing loops

Standard practice when drawing a causal loop diagram:

Name each variable as a noun phrase that can increase or decrease (for example "project rework", not "rework is high").

Draw an arrow from each cause to each effect.

Label every arrow with + or - to show the causal direction.

Mark any arrow where the effect is delayed with // across it.

Label each closed loop R or B, using the negative-link rule.

Worked Examples

Classifying a loop with three negative links

Suppose a closed loop contains three links marked negative. Three is odd, so by the negative-link rule the loop is balancing (B). Intuitively, each negative link reverses the direction of change; three reversals leave the loop pushing back against whatever change started it.

Classifying a loop with no negative links

A loop in which every link is positive contains zero negative links. Zero counts as even, so the loop is reinforcing (R): a change travelling around the loop comes back amplified in the same direction.

A reinforcing loop of decline

Because a reinforcing loop amplifies change in whichever direction it is already moving, the same loop structure can drive a runaway decline. If an initial deterioration triggers effects that further increase the deterioration, the R loop accelerates the downward spiral exactly as it would accelerate growth. This is why a reinforcing loop should never be read as "good growth" by default.
